To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the majority of patients would prefer to receive their radiology report directly from the radiologist, and (2) radiology departments should develop a strategy to provide patients with direct access to their radiology reports.

radiologists should communicate directly with patients in cases where the referring physician does not receive the radiology report, and that this may present an opportunity for radiologists to strengthen their role in the patient's care.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the radiologist should communicate with the patient directly if there is a discrepancy in the patient's medical history, if the patient has not been informed of an abnormality, if a patient is not satisfied with the communication of his or her physician, if the patient requests a second opinion, if the radiologist believes that the patient should know of a finding, or if the patient has a life-threatening abnormality.
radiologists should communicate with patients directly when it is in the patient's interest to do so.
the radiologist has a duty to report to the patient any findings that would be considered significant if they were found in a nonimaging modality study.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the radiologist should be the first to communicate results to a patient and that the radiologist is the best person to explain the findings.
the current system for communicating results is broken.
radiologists have a legal and professional responsibility to communicate with patients.
The main takeaway from our work is that
direct patient communication is a viable option for radiologists who want to ensure that patients are aware of important findings, but who do not have a relationship with a referring physician.
radiologists should be aware that patients have a right to access their medical records, including radiology reports.
radiologists should not be afraid of direct communication with patients and should be prepared to do so when necessary.
